E1046.summary: Maker of the perpetual lamp found near Alestes, whose urn inscription Atwood cites as speaking of elements digested by laborious art.
E1046.body: Named as the maker of a perpetual lamp found near Alestes [I.1 ¶18]. His urn inscription is cited for its line about elements enclosed and digested by heavy labour: “Namque elementa gravi clausit digesta labore” [I.1 ¶19]. Our rendering (by: ours): for he enclosed the elements, digested with heavy labour. Atwood cites it for its mention of elements digested by laborious art.

E1047.summary: In an Indian record Atwood quotes, whatever appears or does not appear in the mind apart from the First Cause: the mind's image or delusion.
E1047.body: A term from a quoted Indian record, not Atwood's own: whatever appears or does not appear in the mind, other than the First Cause, is to be known as “the mind’s maya (or image or delusion) as of light or darkness” [II.3 ¶48]. The gloss “image or delusion” is the text's own.

E1048.summary: The meadow of Divine Ideas: the prolific power of life and the grasp of the first efficient causes of life and Forms; the Alchemists call it their garden.
E1048.body: Atwood, drawing on Plato, says “the Meadow is the prolific power of life, according to Plato” [II.4 ¶16]; she describes it as the comprehension of the first efficient causes of life and of Forms. She identifies it with the Alchemists' garden: “this meadow of Divine Ideas, or Pratum, as the Oracle denotes it, is a place well known to philosophers; the Alchemists in general call it their garden” [II.4 ¶9]. So in her reading the Platonic/Oracular Meadow (Pratum) and the alchemical garden name the same place.

E1049.summary: In Hermes as quoted, the third product from the Stone after water and gold, nobler than the water with the faeces.
E1049.body: Hermes, as quoted, lists it as the third product from the Stone: “the third is our almost or medial gold which is more noble than the water with the faeces” [I.3 ¶55]. The text does not explain it further.

E1050.summary: The middle or second life, between the mineral and the higher life, reached by dissolving the sensuous medium, through which the third life is raised and born.
E1050.body:
Atwood's term for an intermediate level of life. Most records come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer).

**In the Appendix.** It is the second life: “Dissolve the sensuous medium and you have the second or medial life.” [APP ¶182]. The third life is born “through the medial or celestial life” [APP ¶35], so it is equated with the celestial life. The exalted spirit is “the spirit in the medial life” [APP ¶15]. When life is drawn inward, “the medial spirit is changed; life is attracted in, instead of out” [APP ¶24]. It sits between the mineral and the higher life; the Salt “must be translated or drawn up into the medial life” [APP ¶77], and the heart centre is “the heart of the celestial medial vegetable life” [APP ¶95]. It is also the life in which we ought to be efficient, so as to be efficient for the divine life above us; Atwood equates this with faith: “efficient in the medial life --- in faith” [APP ¶45].

**In the main text.** In the order of the Mysteries, “Close upon the revealment of the Medial Life then, as we take it, in order of the Mysteries followed the Purificative Rites” [II.2 ¶20]; the passage does not define it. Following the Platonists, the generative virtue forms an “intellectual alliance with the medial life and light” [III.2 ¶9]. Atwood glosses Enoch's wooden receptacles as this life: “the wooden receptacles (the vegetable or medial life)” [III.2 ¶12].

Whether the II.2 usage means the same as the Appendix's second life is not stated.

E1051.summary: The senses' own light, in which they are entranced at the start of the practice.
E1051.body: Atwood speaks of “entrancing the senses in their own medial light” [IV.1 ¶3] at the start of the practice. The text gives no further gloss.

E1052.summary: The middle region of life into which the hidden Sulphur must be transplanted before it can grow and become manifest.
E1052.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says the Sulphur “has to be drawn forth and transplanted into the medial region before it can grow and become manifest” [APP ¶125], and that something follows “When the medial life draws the hidden central light” [APP ¶125]. The context suggests the medial region is the place of the medial life (see medial life).

E1053.summary: A spirit whose forms and properties are extinguished in the fermentation; not further explained.
E1053.body: Atwood describes the fermentation as taking place “by an extinguishing of the forms and properties of the Medial Spirit” [III.2 ¶28]. It is not explained further here; compare the Appendix's “medial spirit” that is changed when life is drawn inward (see medial life).

E1054.summary: In the Lucerna Salis as quoted, the means by which God grants the art: instruction and the labour of the hands.
E1054.body: The author of the Lucerna Salis, as quoted, says God grants the art not immediately “but always by mediate dispositions, to wit, by instructions and the labour of the hands” [III.4 ¶20].

E1055.summary: The transmuting and healing product of the work, the Stone in its tinging form, whose virtue grows with each dissolution and multiplication.
E1055.body:
The medicine is the agent that transmutes metals and also heals. Its strength is spoken of as its height or virtue: “the true height of the medicine” [I.1 ¶66]; “the White medicine of sufficient virtue to convert 120,000 times its weight into the purest silver” [I.1 ¶73], also called a tincture in the same account [I.1 ¶73].

**Quoted authorities.** The Lucerna Solis and the monk of the Rosary make it from the salt of the world and call it one thing: “the medicine is one, in which the whole mystery consists” [I.2 ¶11]; “Of it is made that medicine which will preserve you from all maladies” [I.2 ¶10]. The Scholiast says the bodies are reduced into it, it tinges 10, 100, 1000 parts, and “the oftener the medicine is dissolved, by so much more it increases in virtue” [I.3 n38]. The Hunting of the Greene Lyon keeps ferment in the fire “That thy Medicine augment mayst aye;” [III.1 ¶65]. The fraternity of the Rosy Cross: “The third gate is the fire which conduceth to the maturity of the medicine.” [III.3 ¶63]; at the fourth gate it is a universal medicine for all diseases. In IV.3 it is the Stone in working form; diluted in mercury “you will have the medicine, though of an inferior order” [IV.3 ¶20]; Vaughan speaks of “the Stone and magic medicine” and calls it “such a subtle moist fire” that only its proper glass can hold it [IV.3 ¶22].

**Atwood.** Philosophers, “when they have obtained this medicine”, did not care to lengthen their days or parade riches [IV.3 ¶48]. She also reports Heraclitus calling the theurgic media medicines: “Heraclitus calls these medicines, as being the help and remedy of imperfect souls” [II.2 ¶5]; these also healed the body.

E1056.summary: A mean or intermediary: the precepts demand one between the two; in the practice, the sensible medium released by entrancing and purified; also any means toward an end.
E1056.body:
The word carries several senses.

**A mean between two.** Hermes, as quoted: “for the precepts demand a medium” [I.3 ¶23]; “the temperate unguent, which is fire, is the medium between the faeces and the water” [I.3 ¶24]. Atwood repeats “for the precepts demand a medium” [III.1 ¶41] as why the two Spirits need each other. Compare “medium and bond”.

**The sensible medium.** Atwood uses it of the mesmeric agent, the photogenic medium. Quoting an adept, one who has the Art “and hath the medium, will be richer than any other” [II.2 ¶18]; the purified principle becomes “the medium of that holy and sublime experience” [II.2 ¶25]. In regeneration “the sensible medium, which in this present birth is dominant, being made occult” [III.1 ¶50]. It is released by entrancing: “the medium in its natural state is volatile, immanifest, phantastic, irrational, and important” [IV.1 ¶4], so it must be purified; there are “many ways of including the sensible medium” [IV.1 ¶5]. In IV.1 ¶7 the word is also used for the means by which the Royal Diadem is extracted.

**A means toward an end.** Aristotle, as quoted: in deliberation “they consider how and by what Medium it may be obtained” [IV.1 ¶30], tracing media back to the first Cause. Atwood applies this: “That Medium, therefore, which is last in the analysis is first in generation” [IV.1 ¶31]; inquiry ends at the medium immediately in the operator's power, and there the work begins. Zachary, quoted: “Mediums nevertheless are to be employed” [III.4 ¶20] besides prayer.

How far these senses are one in Atwood's mind is not stated.

E1057.summary: What Atwood says any increase of the Spirit requires.
E1057.body: Atwood: “neither is there any increase of the Spirit, as we have already shown, without a medium and a bond” [III.4 ¶30]. See medium.

E1058.summary: Improvement: the natural life needs it, and the operator must have its principles in himself.
E1058.body: Atwood speaks of “how much such a life is in need of melioration” [II.2 ¶18], and of those “wanting the very principles of melioration in themselves” [II.2 ¶29], meaning the operator must have these principles within.

E1059.summary: Reported via Aristotle as holding the One according to Matter; the view is dismissed as rustic.
E1059.body: Known in the text only through Aristotle's report: Melissus takes the One according to Matter, a view dismissed as rustic [III.2 ¶40].

E1060.summary: A figure teaching the hidden mysteries of creation to the young Aspirant, apparently by inward evolution rather than words.
E1060.body: Atwood uses the Memphian prophet as the teacher of the hidden mysteries of creation to the young Aspirant, apparently by inward evolution rather than by words [III.3 ¶44].

E1061.summary: In Eirenaeus as quoted, one of three menstruals; the freed fire appears visibly in the third, which only one who knows the first two can see.
E1061.body: Eirenaeus, as quoted, speaks of three menstruals. The freed fire “appears visibly in our Third Menstrual” [III.1 ¶14], but “he that knows not our two first menstruals is altogether shut out” [III.1 ¶14]. The text does not say what the menstruals are.

E1062.summary: What 'that water' must be: drawn out of the sphere of the Moon and rectified until it can calcine gold.
E1062.body: In a passage of uncertain voice: “Now that water must be the menstruum of the world” [IV.3 ¶21], “out of the sphere of the Moon so often rectified until it can calcine gold” [IV.3 ¶21]. It is not explained further.

E1063.summary: In Eudoxus as quoted, the viscous water into which the secret fire's water dissolves; the beginning, foundation and Key of the Art.
E1063.body: Eudoxus, as quoted: the water drawn out by the secret fire, through magical union with the dry water of the sea of the wise, “is dissolved into a viscous water -- into a mercurial liquor” [IV.3 ¶16], “a mercurial liquor, which is the beginning, the foundation, and the Key of our Art” [IV.3 ¶16]. It is thus equated with the viscous water. See Mercury.

E1064.summary: In Ripley as quoted, said of mineral and metallic bodies reduced to their beginning; apparently 'turned into mercury'.
E1064.body: Ripley, as quoted: “Mineral and metalline may be mercurizate” [I.2 ¶6], said of fusible bodies once reduced to their beginning. The text does not gloss the word; the context suggests made into mercury in the philosophers' sense (see Mercury).

E1065.summary: One of the three principles with Sulphur and Salt; in the philosophers' sense the first matter, a living spirit-water, not common mercury, in which the art begins and ends.
E1065.body:
**Not common mercury.** The philosophers never teach that “mercury as mercury specificate, can be changed into gold” [I.2 ¶4]. Their Mercury is the first matter to which bodies are reduced: “reduce the body into water, that is, into mercury” [I.2 ¶5], also called argent vive [I.2 ¶5]; it is the root of gold and silver [I.2 ¶11]; “All is in Mercury which the wise men seek” [I.2 ¶12] (Bacon, Rosarium, Geber, Aquinas, endorsed by Atwood). Atwood: “the Mercury of the philosophers is not found of itself on earth” [I.2 ¶49]; it is “the Universal Spirit or Mercury” [I.2 ¶49], also called Proteus and quintessence [I.2 ¶37]; the preparation includes “multiplying the Mercury by its proper Light” [I.2 ¶39]. Albertus calls it permanent water, unctuous vapour and spirit of body [I.2 ¶29]; Lully calls it Hyle [I.2 ¶29].

**Living agent.** The Scholiast: “philosophic, fiery, vital, running” [I.3 n9]; the art begins and “finishes in the same” [I.3 n55]. The adepts call it “the recreated body of the spirit, passive and pure” and “the earth of the wise” [I.3 n29]. After preparation the vulgar Matter becomes “pure, agile, intelligent, living” [II.2 ¶16]. Atwood: it is “the impure vapor of life” that the sulphuric Spirit putrefies [III.1 ¶24]. The Alchemists say it comes only “by help of ingenuity and industry” [III.1 ¶13]; Lully, by ingenuity and manual operation [IV.1 ¶5]. Boehme, Agrippa and Paracelsus' disciples: “the Mercurial Spirit is everywhere” [II.1 ¶9], though not equally extractable from all. Eiraneaus: separating light from darkness seven times, “the creation of the philosophic mercury will be complete” [I.3 n39]. Eudoxus: its whole energy lies in “the fixed salt of our compound” [IV.3 ¶9].

**Identities.** Atwood: in the first conjunction the Spirit predominates, in the second its Light, “which two are, by adepts, called Mercury and Gold” [III.3 ¶30]. Eirenaeus: “This is our water, this our secret fire.” [III.1 ¶69], the first matter of metals, a water dry. Grasseus: quicksilver, the same as Lully's Lunaria [III.2 ¶25]. The Rosy Cross Dragon: “I am called of the philosophers Mercury: my husband is Gold philosophical.” [III.3 ¶64], also Egg and Light of nature. Eudoxus: “Our Old Man is our Mercury” [IV.3 ¶10], first matter and water of metals, white and red, carrying “in its centre its own Sulphur” [IV.3 ¶12]; “the Spirit, which is our Mercury” [IV.3 ¶12]. Sendivogius: the water into which earth is resolved [IV.3 ¶21]. Atwood names it with the Sal Sepientum [II.4 ¶39], and Behmen's Mercurius as “spirit of the Sound” [APP ¶49, Appendix layer].

**In the work.** The adept: it rises “to her superior habitation” [III.3 ¶17]. The author of The Triumph: it is whitened, citrined and fed “with its own blood” [IV.2 ¶6]; the theosophist says it “doth all this itself” as “the workman which is in it already” [IV.3 ¶38]. The bottomless Mercury of Eirenaeus [III.1 ¶19; APP ¶89] is not decoded. Whether the fixed philosopher's Mercury of III.3 ¶32 is the same as Mercury-as-Spirit is open.

E1066.summary: Planetary properties to which perception and intuition belong: clearer in enunciation than the emotional spheres, weaker in feeling and realization.
E1066.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood assigns “perception or intuition, which are the property of Mercury and Jupiter” [APP ¶113]; these are clearer in enunciation than the emotional spheres but weaker in feeling and realization.

E1067.summary: In the Open Entrance as quoted, what is added, three or four parts to one of Perfect Matter, in Multiplication.
E1067.body: The Author of the Open Entrance, as quoted, directs adding “three or four parts at most of the Mercury of the First Work” [IV.3 ¶18] to one part of the Perfect Matter in Multiplication. Not further defined.

E1068.summary: Listed among the great spirits; his Prophecies are reported to refer solely to Hermetic arcana, and Norton names him among masters who wrote obscurely.
E1068.body: Atwood lists Merlin (given as St Ambrose) among the great spirits, and reports that his Prophecies refer solely to Hermetic arcana [I.1 ¶39, I.1 ¶45, I.1 n54]. Norton's verse names him with Hermes, Rasis, Geber, Avicen, Hortolan, Democrit, Morien, Bacon and Raymond as masters who “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15].

E1069.summary: The modern art that uses the same agent as the Mysteries but for inferior ends; Atwood's first key and Door-keeper to the vestibule of antique science.
E1069.body:
Atwood treats Mesmerism as a real but external, preliminary form of the same art. It works with the same agent, but “the object was different and immeasurably superior to those proposed by modern Mesmerism” [II.2 ¶24]. In its preliminary practice “the modern art, called Mesmerism, strikingly accords” with the Mysteries and Alchemy [IV.4 ¶5].

She ranks it as a beginning only: “This Mesmerism, in respect of our Mystery then, may be regarded as a first key” [III.1 ¶8], one that opens only into the vestibule and shows the labyrinth of life, since its practitioners mesmerize one another without knowing how to amend the Thing. “Mesmerism, as it is mechanically practiced in the present day, is a first step indeed” [IV.3 ¶37] before the temple of Divine Wisdom.

She credits it personally: “We allude to Mesmerism: not ashamed, but grateful to acknowledge the neglected Door-keeper” [III.4 ¶13], “the neglected Door-keeper that gave us first introduction to the vestibule of antique science” [III.4 ¶13]; it relieves suffering and offers the multitude a new guide to knowledge and felicity.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “The action of mesmerism is a very external way” [APP ¶73]: by vertical passes it loosens spirit from its corporeal media for the moment, an external imitation of the Divine Art of separation.

E1070.summary: Mentioned as reviving belief in an Odic Force, which Atwood does not assume, and as having Aesculapius as its only just pride.
E1070.body: Atwood notes that the phenomena of Mesmerism have revived belief in an Odic Force, which she does not assume here [I.2 ¶16]. Elsewhere she says Aesculapius is its only just pride [IV.3 ¶36]; whether this is praise or a limitation is unclear. See the main Mesmerism entry.

E1071.summary: What the soul is said to be: a mesothesis between two spheres, its ultimate perfection.
E1071.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says of the soul: “it is its ultimate perfection, for it is a mesothesis between two spheres” [APP ¶178]. The term is not glossed; the context suggests a middle position between two spheres.

E1072.summary: Something whose breaking precedes the birth of the Elias spirit; not explained.
E1072.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “When the metal bond is broken” [APP ¶139], the Elias spirit is born. Not explained further.

E1073.summary: What Atwood says the soul's angelic essence is.
E1073.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “The soul’s angelic essence is a metallic humidity.” [APP ¶181]. Not explained further.

E1074.summary: The perfection reached in metals, belonging only to the primary evolution of life and distinct from the ultimate Divine association.
E1074.body: Atwood speaks of “the metalline perfection, which belongs to the primary evolution of life only” [IV.3 ¶27], and warns against confusing it with the ultimate Divine association.

E1075.summary: The metallic root, which appears first in the experimental process and is most easily apportioned.
E1075.body: Atwood: “the metalline radix first presents itself in the experimental process” [I.2 ¶49], and it is the most easily apportioned.
